newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Post-payroll pause, then data.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Post-payroll pause, then data.

text.p: The U.S. bond market passed a major test on Friday, rallying in the wake of another strong month of job growth in February.

Players said the market should take a breather for the first part of the upcoming week, as it awaits the next round of key economic reports on Thursday and Friday: retail sales, producer prices and industrial production.
"I don't think we'll do anything until then," said a head trader with a U.S. primary dealership. "The rally has run its course until then."

Friday afternoon, the 30-year bond was at 97-20/32, up 28/32, while its yield fell to 6.81 percent. Just after the Labor Department reported a 339,000 gain in February nonfarm payrolls, the bond fell about one point, but recovered on muted wage pressures.

Until there are noticeable signs of inflationary pressures, "you won't get any selling pressure to push yields appreciably higher," said William Sullivan, director of money markets research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. As such, the market has begun to factor out a Fed tightening later this month, though a rate rise in May is very much in the picture.

Since the odds of a tightening sometime soon is forecast, "I think the market has a great understanding that it will have trouble pushing (long bond) rates to seven percent," said Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.

He noted that the long end in particular is seemingly pleased with the lack of current inflationary pressures and Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's tough talk, warning of a pre-emptive strike.
"It behooves to own bonds," Platt said, adding that bond market inflows remain strong.
Market participants said Treasuries should stay 10 to 15 basis points below the peaks of the past couple months.
But retail sales, due Thursday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, pose the biggest problem, as a combination of quicker tax refunds and bonus payments could push the data higher than expected.
Both overall retail sales and sales ex-autos are expected to rise 0.6 percent in February, a poll by Reuters shows.

"We're going to get a moderate to strong number," Platt said, noting that revisions to prior months will be equally significant. It's the number (of the week) with the most potential for an upward surprise."
On Friday, the February producer price index will be released at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, followed 45 minutes later by the Fed's industrial production data for February.

The PPI is expected to have fallen 0.1 percent, while the PPI core rate is seen down 0.3 percent in February, the Reuters poll showed. Further, industrial production is seen up 0.5 percent, with the capacity utilization rate up 0.2 point to 83.5 percent.
Some noted that, while the market could fall on Thursday should retail sales be strong, it would rebound on Friday on tame inflation numbers.

Also in the upcoming week, fourth-quarter productivity and wholesale inventories data are scheduled for release Tuesday and the Fed's Beige Book is due Wednesday -- all of which are seen having a limited effect on the market.
